paragraphs.heading: The energy of moving things
paragraphs.text: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving. In classical mechanics, a non-rotating object of mass m going at speed v has a kinetic energy of 1/2mv². Energy is measured in joules in the SI system and in foot-pounds in the English system. The word kinetic comes from the Greek kinesis, which means motion.

paragraphs.heading: Work in, work out
paragraphs.text: To bring an object from rest up to its speed, you have to do work on it, meaning a force along the direction of motion multiplied by the distance moved. The kinetic energy it ends up with equals exactly that work. When the object slows back down to a stop, it does the same amount of work itself. In relativistic mechanics, 1/2mv² is a good stand-in only when the speed is far below the speed of light. And like anything that depends on velocity, kinetic energy depends on how the object relates to the observer's frame of reference, so it is not invariant.

paragraphs.heading: A ride on a bicycle
paragraphs.text: A cyclist who speeds up turns chemical energy from food into kinetic energy of rider and bike. On flat ground she can hold that speed without more work, apart from pushing against air resistance and friction. The change is not perfectly efficient, and some energy ends up as heat inside her body. If she coasts up a hill and stops right at the top, most of her kinetic energy has become gravitational potential energy, which she gets back by freewheeling down. Friction takes some along the way, so without pedaling she never quite regains her full speed; that energy was not destroyed, only changed into another form. If she brakes instead, friction turns her kinetic energy into heat.

paragraphs.heading: Passing it along
paragraphs.text: Kinetic energy can move from one object to another. In billiards, the cue stick gives the cue ball kinetic energy. When that ball hits another, it slows sharply while the struck ball speeds off with the energy. These hits are effectively elastic collisions, in which kinetic energy is kept. In inelastic collisions, it is spread into other forms such as heat, sound and the energy of breaking structures apart.

paragraphs.heading: Up in orbit
paragraphs.text: A spacecraft uses chemical energy at launch to build up a lot of kinetic energy and reach orbital velocity. In a perfectly circular orbit that kinetic energy stays the same, since there is almost no friction in space near Earth. It shows itself again at re-entry, when some of it becomes heat. On an elliptical orbit, kinetic and potential energy keep trading places: kinetic energy peaks at the closest approach and is lowest at the farthest point. Leaving aside any loss or gain, their sum stays constant.

paragraphs.heading: Living force
paragraphs.text: Gottfried Leibniz and Johann Bernoulli developed the principle that E ∝ mv² is conserved, and they called this energy vis viva, the living force. In 1722 Willem 's Gravesande dropped weights from different heights into clay and found that how deep they sank was proportional to the square of their speed at impact. Émilie du Châtelet saw what the experiment meant and published an explanation. Thomas Young, in an 1802 lecture to the Royal Society, used the word energy for kinetic energy in its modern sense, and William Thomson is credited with coining the term kinetic energy around 1849 to 1851.
